# velamen

> Python library and CLI for steganography over LLM token probability distributions: arithmetic coding over a pre-frozen table of top-5 token probabilities (a `.hchan` file), with optional ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, plus HCTP, a hash-chained context transfer format implemented from draft-ruvalcaba-hctp-01. Apache-2.0.

If a command, tool or endpoint is not listed in this file, it does not exist in velamen. The complete public surface is: the `velamen` CLI with exactly four subcommands (`freeze`, `verify`, `encode`, `decode`), and the Python API `encode`, `decode`, `freeze`, `verify`, `ContextChain`, `ContextBlock`, `SyncPacket`, `AckPacket`, `HctpSender`, `HctpReceiver` (all exported from `velamen/__init__.py`). There is no network service and no other entry point.

Facts agents often get wrong: it is not on PyPI (install from git only, `pip install "velamen[crypto] @ git+https://github.com/saluca-labs/velamen@<ref>"`); encode and decode need no model, only the shared `.hchan` file; `velamen freeze` needs a local Ollama and, as of 2026-10-22, did not produce a usable channel in the one configuration tested (see the README correction); the cover text is not shown to be indistinguishable from model output. "Hermes" in docs/PROTOCOL.md names the stego transport that velamen/stego.py implements. Python 3.10+, one runtime dependency (`requests`).

The full text of this repository's prose docs, concatenated, each under its path. Regenerate this file whenever one of them changes.

## README.md

### Velamen

Steganographic communication over LLM token probability distributions: a Python library and CLI that hides a message in generated-looking text by arithmetic coding over a pre-frozen table of token probabilities.

Velamen encodes secret messages into LLM-style text using arithmetic coding over pre-frozen token probability distributions. Both sides hold the same frozen `.hchan` channel file, so no live model is needed at encode or decode time.

> **Correction, 2026-10-22.** This README said "The cover text is indistinguishable from normal model output." That is not established and does not hold by construction. Each position's distribution is frozen along the model's greedy path, but the encoder then picks tokens other than the greedy one, so later tokens are drawn from distributions conditioned on text that was never emitted. The table also keeps only the top 5 tokens per position, renormalised. No detectability evaluation exists in this repo. See also the second correction under [Quickstart](#quickstart).

#### Status

Experimental (version 0.2.0). What works today, measured 2026-10-22 on `origin/main` at `213c107` (stego) and 2026-11-11 (HCTP):

- `encode` / `decode` round-trip, raw and encrypted, on a channel file: the stego tests in `tests/test_stego.py` pass on Python 3.12, and `examples/basic_usage.py` round-trips on a synthetic channel.
- HCTP implements [draft-ruvalcaba-hctp-01](docs/PROTOCOL.md): canonical RFC 8785 block encoding, the ordered receiver checks, and the sender's frozen window, split parts and ACK check. It reproduces the draft's Appendix A vectors and Konrad Gruszka's independent fold, encoding and packet vectors (`tests/test_hctp01_vectors.py`). The fixed SYNC overhead is 74 bytes. See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md): 0.2.0 does not interoperate with 0.1.0 on non-ASCII context.
- `velamen freeze` against a real Ollama model did not produce a usable channel in the one configuration tested (see the correction below). Treat channel freezing as not working until that is fixed.

#### Install

Velamen is distributed as source from this GitHub repository only. It is not
published on PyPI; never install a package of this name from PyPI, it is not ours.
Install from git, pinned to a tag or commit you have reviewed (the commit below is
an example; replace it with the ref you want):

```bash
pip install "velamen @ git+https://github.com/saluca-labs/velamen@2d992c1a6157710227af792d43b89a034913491b"
# For encrypted channels (recommended):
pip install "velamen[crypto] @ git+https://github.com/saluca-labs/velamen@2d992c1a6157710227af792d43b89a034913491b"
```

Tested 2026-10-22 with Python 3.12.10 on Windows 11 (`cryptography` 50.0.2, `requests` 2.34.2). CI runs Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12. Requirements:

- Python 3.10+
- `cryptography` (optional, needed for encrypted mode)
- [Ollama](https://ollama.com), for `velamen freeze` only

For development, from a clone:

```bash
pip install -e ".[crypto,dev]"
python -m pytest tests/ -v
```

#### Quickstart

The shortest run that produces a visible result needs no model. From a clone:

```bash
python examples/basic_usage.py
```

It builds a synthetic channel (hand-written distributions inside the script), then encodes and decodes in raw and encrypted mode. Excerpt of a real run, 2026-10-22:

```text
--- 2. Raw Mode (no encryption) ---
  Encoding without encryption -- useful for testing and inspection.

  Secret message:  'Attack at dawn'
  Cover text:      The system shows clear in the data and also shows The system shows clear...
  Cover length:    1007 chars
  Decoded message: 'Attack at dawn'
  Match:           YES
```

The full output is in [Screenshots](#screenshots).

> **Correction, 2026-10-22.** This README presented `velamen freeze` followed by `velamen encode --msg "attack at dawn"` as a working quick start. On 2026-10-22 it did not work in the configuration tested. With Ollama 0.34.4 and `gemma2:9b` (the README's `phi3:mini` was not available on the test machine and was not tested), a 200-position freeze produced a channel whose greedy text was the single token `Please` repeated, with a capacity of about 10 bytes, and `encode` refused the message:
>
> ```text
> $ velamen freeze --prompt "The quarterly earnings report indicated that" --model gemma2:9b --tokens 200 --out channel.hchan
> Freezing 200 positions for model 'gemma2:9b'...
> (progress line omitted)
> Done. 200 positions in 33.1s
> Channel saved: channel.hchan
> Fingerprint:  f5d335d16d377a7a6cba39617856093db659ac53a30eedf16d2527b061bc87bd
> Capacity:     ~2 bytes
> $ velamen encode --msg "attack at dawn" --channel channel.hchan --key "shared-secret"
> ValueError: Message too large: 400 bits needed, channel holds ~84 bits (10.5 bytes)
> ```
>
> The likely cause is in `velamen/channel.py`: `_query_top_k` calls Ollama's `/api/chat` with the growing text as a *user* message and `num_predict: 1`, so each position is the first token of a fresh assistant reply rather than the next token of a continuation. An encrypted message needs 36 bytes of overhead (4 length, 12 nonce, 16 tag, 4 guard) plus the message itself, so "attack at dawn" needs 50 bytes of capacity. Two freezes with identical arguments on the same machine also gave different channels (81 and 84 bits of capacity), so frozen channels are not reproducible from the prompt alone; exchange the `.hchan` file itself.

#### Usage

##### CLI

```bash
velamen freeze --prompt "<seed text>" --model <ollama model> --tokens 200 --out channel.hchan
velamen verify channel.hchan
velamen encode --msg "<message>" --channel channel.hchan --key "<shared passphrase>"
velamen decode --cover "<cover text>" --channel channel.hchan --key "<shared passphrase>"
```

`--raw` on `encode` / `decode` skips encryption; use it only for testing. `freeze` takes `--ollama <url>` (default `http://localhost:11434`). `verify` recomputes the SHA-256 fingerprint of the distributions and prints `Integrity: PASS` or `FAIL` (exit 1 on FAIL), as in the real run below on the channel frozen above:

```text
$ velamen verify channel.hchan
File:        channel.hchan
Fingerprint: f5d335d16d377a7a6cba39617856093db659ac53a30eedf16d2527b061bc87bd
Integrity:   PASS
Model:       gemma2:9b
Positions:   200
Capacity:    ~2 bytes
```

##### Python API

```python
import json
from velamen import encode, decode

with open("channel.hchan") as f:
    channel = json.load(f)

cover = encode("secret message", channel, key="shared-key")
recovered = decode(cover, channel, key="shared-key")
assert recovered == "secret message"
```

`examples/encrypted_channel.py` shows an encrypted exchange between two parties and an eavesdropper with the wrong key, plus HCTP state sync, on a synthetic channel.

##### HCTP: Hash-Chain Context Transfer Protocol

Velamen is the reference implementation of HCTP as specified in the Internet-Draft draft-ruvalcaba-hctp-01: a protocol for transferring conversational context as compact, tamper-evident, hash-chained payloads. Only blocks not yet acknowledged cross the wire; acknowledged history is a 32-byte root hash.

```python
from velamen import HctpSender, HctpReceiver

tx, rx = HctpSender(), HctpReceiver()
tx.add_turn("user", "What is the mission status?", "asked about mission status")
tx.add_turn("agent", "All systems nominal.", "confirmed systems nominal")

wire_bytes = tx.build_sync().serialize()  # 74 bytes + compressed delta
result = rx.receive(wire_bytes)           # the draft's ordered receiver checks
tx.receive_ack(result.ack_bytes)          # 38-byte ACK; both roots now agree
```

This SYNC serialises to 280 bytes (74 fixed plus the compressed delta) in a 2026-11-11 run. HCTP has no confidentiality or peer authentication of its own; carry it over an authenticated, encrypted transport. See [docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md) for how velamen maps to the draft.

##### Security

- **Encryption**: ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD (via the `cryptography` package)
- **Key derivation**: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 100,000 iterations, fixed salt `velamen-channel-v1`
- **Integrity**: HCTP hash chains provide tamper-evident session history
- **Channel security**: frozen distributions are a pre-shared secret; the `.hchan` file must be exchanged securely

#### Architecture

1. **Freeze** (`velamen/channel.py`): query an Ollama model for the top-5 token log-probabilities at each position along a greedy path and save them, with a SHA-256 fingerprint and a capacity estimate, as a `.hchan` JSON file.
2. **Encode** (`velamen/stego.py`): prefix the message (or its ChaCha20-Poly1305 ciphertext) with a 4-byte length, treat the bits as an arithmetic-coded stream, and expand them into tokens chosen from the frozen distributions.
3. **Decode** (`velamen/stego.py`): split the cover text back into tokens by longest match against each position's distribution, re-compress to bits, read the length, and decrypt.

The same frozen distributions (`channel.hchan`) drive both directions. Encoding a message runs
the arithmetic coder in its decompression direction (bits out to tokens), and decoding runs it in
its compression direction (tokens back to bits); both functions live in `velamen/stego.py`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  H[(channel.hchan<br/>frozen top-5 distributions)]

  subgraph encode["encode() path"]
    direction LR
    M1[message] --> EN["_encrypt + 4-byte length prefix"]
    EN --> B1["_bytes_to_bits"]
    B1 --> TK["_bits_to_tokens<br/>(arithmetic coder, decompress)"]
    TK --> C1[cover text]
  end

  subgraph decode["decode() path"]
    direction LR
    C2[cover text] --> TB["_tokens_to_bits<br/>(longest-match, then compress)"]
    TB --> B2["_bits_to_bytes + strip length"]
    B2 --> DE["_decrypt"]
    DE --> M2[message]
  end

  H --> TK
  H --> TB
```

Key files: `velamen/cli.py` (CLI), `velamen/stego.py` (coding and crypto), `velamen/channel.py` (freeze and verify), `velamen/hctp.py` (HCTP), `docs/PROTOCOL.md` (HCTP as implemented from draft-ruvalcaba-hctp-01; "Hermes" there names the stego transport that `velamen/stego.py` implements).

## docs/PROTOCOL.md

### HCTP - Hash-Chain Context Transfer Protocol

velamen implements **draft-ruvalcaba-hctp-01**, the Internet-Draft that specifies HCTP. The
draft is normative; this page summarises it and says where each rule lives in
`velamen/hctp.py`. Where this page and the draft differ, the draft governs. Section numbers
below are the draft's.

HCTP transfers an ordered, append-only sequence of conversational context between two
endpoints. Acknowledged history is a single 32-byte rolling hash (the static root); only the
blocks not yet acknowledged (the dynamic window) are sent. HCTP carries no confidentiality and
no peer authentication of its own: run it inside a transport that provides both. In velamen
that is the encrypted stego channel (called "Hermes" in older notes, implemented by
`velamen/stego.py`), and any authenticated transport such as TLS 1.3 or QUIC works equally.

---

#### Context block (Section 3.1)

```
{"content_hash":"<64 lowercase hex>","role":"<1..64 octets>","seq":<uint32>,"summary":"<0..120 code points>"}
```

- `seq`: position in its directional chain, starting at 0.
- `role`: an application label, 1 to 64 octets of UTF-8. It never selects a chain.
- `content_hash`: SHA-256 of the UTF-8 raw turn text, exactly 64 lowercase hex digits.
- `summary`: at most 120 Unicode code points (a character outside the BMP counts once).
- No Unicode normalization is applied anywhere; NFC and NFD forms of the same text hash
  differently.

##### Canonical encoding

`canonical(B)` is the RFC 8785 (JCS) serialization of the four-member object:

- members in code-point order (`content_hash`, `role`, `seq`, `summary`), no whitespace;
- strings: only `"`, `\` and U+0000..U+001F are escaped. U+0008, U+0009, U+000A, U+000C and
  U+000D use `\b \t \n \f \r`; the other control characters use `\u00xx` with lowercase hex.
  Everything else, including non-ASCII, `<`, `>`, `&`, U+007F, U+2028 and U+2029, is written
  as raw UTF-8. A string with an unpaired surrogate has no canonical form and is refused;
- `seq`: ASCII digits only, no sign, no leading zero (except `0`), no fraction, no exponent.

Several blocks travel as the canonical array: `[`, the canonical blocks joined by `,`, `]`.

In code: `ContextBlock.canonical_bytes()`, `encode_block_array()`, and `parse_block_array()`,
which accepts decompressed octets only if they are exactly the canonical encoding of a
non-empty array of valid blocks.

**Changed from -00.** velamen 0.1.0 wrote non-ASCII as `\uXXXX` (Python's `json.dumps`
default). Under -01 any block with a non-ASCII role or summary folds to a different root than
it did in 0.1.0. ASCII-only blocks fold to the same roots as before.

---

#### Rolling root (Section 4)

```
root_0     = SHA256("hctp-genesis-v1")            15 ASCII octets, no NUL
fold(R, B) = SHA256(R || SHA256(canonical(B)))
```

In code: `genesis_root()` and `fold()`.

---

#### Wire format (Section 5)

All integers are big-endian.

SYNC (`SyncPacket`), 74 octets plus `dynamic_len`:

| Field         | Octets      | Content                                               |
|---------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| version       | 1           | 0x01                                                  |
| ptype         | 1           | 0x53 ('S')                                            |
| seq           | 4           | seq of the last block in dynamic_data                 |
| static_root   | 32          | sender's static root                                  |
| dynamic_len   | 4           | length of dynamic_data, never zero                    |
| dynamic_data  | dynamic_len | one zlib stream, FDICT clear, of the canonical array  |
| combined_hash | 32          | SHA256(static_root \|\| dynamic_data)                 |

ACK (`AckPacket`), exactly 38 octets: version 0x01, ptype 0x41 ('A'), the echoed seq, and
`new_root`, the receiver's static root after folding.

A transport unit carries exactly one packet and nothing else (Section 10). `parse_packet()`
enforces that and reports a `PacketError.reason` of `too_short`, `unknown_version`,
`unknown_packet_type`, `dynamic_len_too_large` or `length_mismatch`. `dynamic_len` is compared
with the receiver's bound before dynamic_data is read.

---

#### Receiver (Sections 6.1, 6.3): `HctpReceiver`

State per directional chain: `local_root`, `last_seen_seq`, `last_block_seq`, `has_seen`,
and `ack_cache` (the cached ACK, the pre-fold root, and the SHA-256 of the accepted SYNC's
octets). `HctpReceiver.receive()` applies the checks in this order:

1. **Framing and version.** Exactly one SYNC filling the transport unit.
2. **Integrity.** combined_hash recomputed over the octets as received.
3. **Replay.** seq below `last_seen_seq` is discarded.
4. **Duplicate.** seq equal to `last_seen_seq`: if the SHA-256 of the received octets equals
   the cached digest, the cached ACK is returned and nothing is folded (a lost ACK); any other
   SYNC with that seq is discarded.
5. **Alignment.** static_root different from `local_root` is fatal: `FatalSessionError`, and
   the session ends.
6. **Ingest validation.** One complete zlib stream with FDICT clear and nothing after it;
   decompressed output within the bound; the octets exactly the canonical non-empty array;
   every block valid; seqs contiguous from `last_block_seq + 1` (or 0); the last block's seq
   equal to the packet seq.
7. **Accept.** Fold, record state, cache `(ACK, pre-fold root, digest)`, return the ACK.

Every non-fatal rejection raises `Rejected` (its `step` names the check) with no state change;
the caller sends nothing. The receiver accepts at least 64 blocks and 65536 decompressed
octets per SYNC (the Section 9 baselines) and refuses to be configured below them.

---

#### Sender (Sections 6.1, 6.2, 6.4, 6.5): `HctpSender`

- `add_turn()` assigns the seq when the block is originated. While a SYNC is outstanding the
  window is frozen and new blocks wait in a queue, already numbered.
- `build_sync()` sends the window, or its first part when it exceeds 64 blocks or 65536
  decompressed octets. The static root does not move at send time.
- `receive_ack()` discards an ACK whose seq is not the outstanding one (or not above
  `last_acked_seq`, which is undefined until the first ACK). Otherwise it folds exactly the
  blocks of the outstanding SYNC into a candidate root. If `new_root` differs, the session
  ends with `FatalSessionError`. If it matches, the root is committed and the SYNC for the
  next part is returned, or, after the last part, queued blocks join the window.
- `retransmit()` returns the outstanding SYNC octet for octet. When the bounded count is
  exhausted the session ends (`SessionEnded`) and all state is discarded.

---

#### Bidirectional sessions and scope (Sections 7, 10)

Each direction is its own chain with its own seq space from 0. An endpoint that both sends and
receives holds one `HctpSender` and one `HctpReceiver`; `ContextChain` bundles the two without
sharing state. The chain a SYNC belongs to is the direction it arrived on, never a block's
`role`. A transport that cannot tell the two directions apart carries only a one-way session.

An HCTP session is bound to one scope instance: one transport connection by default, or an
enclosing session defined by the carrying protocol. Create new objects when that instance ends
(or call `end()`), and never reset them while it continues. A fresh receiver cannot tell an
old first SYNC from a new one, so session freshness is the transport's job.

---

#### Security notes (Section 11)

- The hashes are unkeyed. They detect corruption and out-of-context packets, not an attacker
  who can forge packets; authenticity and confidentiality come from the transport.
- No non-repudiation: either side can build a valid-looking chain from the genesis root.
- A summary can reveal what a turn said, and a content_hash lets anyone confirm a guessed
  plaintext. Encrypt the transport when that matters.
- Decompression is bounded by output size and block count, and dynamic_len is bounded before
  any read.

---

#### Example

```python
from velamen import HctpSender, HctpReceiver

tx, rx = HctpSender(), HctpReceiver()
tx.add_turn("user", raw_text="...", summary="asked about X")

wire = tx.build_sync().serialize()        # send these octets over the transport
result = rx.receive(wire)                 # the peer runs the Section 6.3 checks
tx.receive_ack(result.ack_bytes)          # 38 octets back; roots now agree
assert tx.static_root == rx.local_root
```

#### Test vectors

`tests/test_hctp01_vectors.py` runs the draft's Appendix A file (`vectors-01.json`, digest
pinned) and Konrad Gruszka's independent fold, encoding and packet vectors (MIT) from
`tests/vectors/`. See `tests/vectors/README.md` for where each file comes from.
